First, I need to identify the apparent magnitudes for irregular galaxies and spiral galaxies from the table.

Irregular galaxies in the table:  
- NGC 5408: magnitude 14.0  
- NGC 5477: magnitude 14.5  

Spiral galaxies in the table:  
- NGC 5457: magnitude 8.7  
- NGC 5474: magnitude 11.9  

The statement says: "irregular galaxy is the object type having 2.1 more apparent magnitude than spiral galaxy."  
"More apparent magnitude" means numerically larger magnitude (since higher magnitude = dimmer object).  

I need to check if there is any irregular galaxy with magnitude exactly 2.1 greater than any spiral galaxy in the table.

Check NGC 5408 (14.0) vs spiral galaxies:  
14.0 − 8.7 = 5.3 (not 2.1)  
14.0 − 11.9 = 2.1 → yes, 14.0 is exactly 2.1 more than 11.9.

Check NGC 5477 (14.5) vs spiral galaxies:  
14.5 − 8.7 = 5.8  
14.5 − 11.9 = 2.6  

So NGC 5408 (irregular) has magnitude 14.0, which is 2.1 more than NGC 5474 (spiral) magnitude 11.9.  

The statement says "irregular galaxy is the object type having 2.1 more apparent magnitude than spiral galaxy" — it doesn’t specify "on average" or "for all", so it’s true if at least one irregular galaxy has exactly 2.1 more magnitude than at least one spiral galaxy. That’s true here.

Final Answer: Yes
